question: How do you initialize a new Git repository in an existing directory?
expected_answer: To turn a directory into a new Git repository, you run the command git init. This command creates a .git directory where Git stores all the project's metadata and object database.

question: How do you get a copy of an existing Git repository from a server?
expected_answer: You use the git clone command to receive a full copy of nearly all data the server has for that project. Unlike other version control systems, Git receives every version of every file for the history of the project by default.

question: What command is used to check which files are in which state within your working directory?
expected_answer: The git status command shows you which files are modified but unstaged, which are staged for the next commit, and which are untracked. It also provides hints on how to move files between these states.

question: How do you record staged snapshots permanently to the Git history?
expected_answer: The git commit command takes the files exactly as they are in the staging area and stores that snapshot permanently in the Git directory. Each commit also stores metadata such as the author's name, email, and a commit message.

question: What is the command to stage changes for the next commit?
expected_answer: The git add command adds content from the working directory into the staging area, also known as the index. This allows you to selectively craft what your next commit snapshot will look like.

question: What is the technical definition of a branch in Git?
expected_answer: A branch in Git is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to one of the commits in your history. The default branch name created by git init is master.

question: How do you create a new branch without switching to it?
expected_answer: You can create a new branch pointer using the git branch command followed by the branch name. This creates a new pointer to the same commit you are currently on.

question: How do you switch from your current branch to another existing branch?
expected_answer: The git checkout command is used to switch to an existing branch. When you switch branches, Git reverts the files in your working directory to look like they did the last time you committed on that branch.

question: What is a shortcut command to create a new branch and switch to it immediately?
expected_answer: You can use the git checkout command with the -b switch to create a new branch and switch to it at the same time. This is a very common operation used when starting work on a new topic or issue.

question: What does the special HEAD pointer represent in Git?
expected_answer: In Git, HEAD is a special pointer that refers to the local branch you are currently working on. It serves as the parent of the next commit you create.

question: What happens during a fast-forward merge?
expected_answer: A fast-forward merge occurs when the commit you are merging in is a direct descendant of the commit you are currently on. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward because there is no divergent work to merge together.

question: How do you merge another branch into your currently checked-out branch?
expected_answer: To integrate changes, you use the git merge command followed by the name of the branch you wish to merge in. If the histories have diverged, Git performs a three-way merge using a common ancestor.

question: What is unique about a merge commit compared to a normal commit?
expected_answer: A merge commit is special because it has more than one parent. It represents a snapshot that results from a three-way merge of different development lines.

question: What occurs if you change the same part of the same file differently in two branches being merged?
expected_answer: Git will encounter a merge conflict and will not be able to merge the branches cleanly. It adds conflict markers to the affected files and requires the user to resolve the differences manually before committing.

question: What is the process of rebasing in Git?
expected_answer: Rebasing involves taking all the changes that were committed on one branch and replaying them on top of another branch. This operation rewinds the head to a common ancestor, saves diffs as temporary patches, and applies them in order on the target branch.

question: What is the primary risk of rebasing commits that have been pushed publicly?
expected_answer: The golden rule of rebasing is to never rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others may have based work on. Rebasing rewritten history that has been shared causes major confusion for collaborators who must then re-merge their own work.

question: How can you stop a rebase that is in progress and return to your original state?
expected_answer: If a rebase becomes too complex or you decide it was a mistake, you can run git rebase --abort. This returns your repository to the exact state it was in before the rebase command was started.

question: What is one major benefit of rebasing over merging when integrating changes?
expected_answer: Rebasing produces a cleaner, linear project history because it makes parallel work appear as if it happened in series. This is often preferred by project maintainers so they can integrate patches with a simple fast-forward.

question: How do you register a new remote repository handle for your project?
expected_answer: You use the git remote add command followed by a shortname and the URL of the repository. This allows you to reference that URL easily using the shortname on the command line.

question: What is the difference between fetching and pulling from a remote?
expected_answer: The git fetch command downloads all data from a remote project that you don't have yet but does not automatically merge it with your work. The git pull command is a combination of fetching and then automatically merging that remote data into your current branch.

question: How do you push your local branch changes to a remote repository?
expected_answer: You use the command git push <remote> <branch> to share your commits. This only works if you have write access to the server and if no one else has pushed changes since your last fetch.

question: What are remote-tracking branches?
expected_answer: Remote-tracking branches are local references that represent the state of branches on a remote repository at the time of your last communication. They act as bookmarks to remind you where the remote branches were last seen.

question: What are the three main sections of a Git project that files reside in?
expected_answer: Files in a Git project exist in the working tree, the staging area (also called the index), and the Git directory. The working tree is your local sandbox, the index stores information for the next commit, and the Git directory holds the metadata and object database.

question: What are the three types of objects Git stores in its object database?
expected_answer: Git's core data store consists of blobs, trees, and commits. Blobs represent file contents, trees represent directory structures and filenames, and commits store metadata and pointers to the root trees.

question: How does Git use the SHA-1 hash for data integrity?
expected_answer: Git checksums everything before it is stored and refers to it by that 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 hash. This makes it impossible to change file or directory contents without Git detecting the corruption or change.

question: What is the purpose of the Git 'index'?
expected_answer: The index, also known as the staging area, is a file that stores information about what will go into your next commit. It acts as a proposed next commit snapshot that Git looks at when you run the commit command.

question: What are 'plumbing' and 'porcelain' commands in Git?
expected_answer: Porcelain commands are the user-friendly subcommands like checkout or branch that users use daily. Plumbing commands are lower-level subcommands designed to be chained together or used in scripts to perform fundamental operations.

question: Describe the Integration-Manager workflow commonly used with tools like GitHub.
expected_answer: In this workflow, every developer has write access to their own public fork and read access to the main canonical repository. They push changes to their fork and then send a pull request to the maintainer, who tests and merges the changes into the main project.

question: What is a topic branch and why is it used?
expected_answer: A topic branch is a short-lived branch created for a single particular feature or bug fix. This technique allows developers to context-switch quickly and keep work isolated in silos until it is ready for code review and merging.

question: How does the Benevolent Dictator workflow operate for very large projects?
expected_answer: This hierarchical workflow involves 'lieutenants' who merge developers' topic branches and a 'dictator' who merges lieutenants' work into a master branch. Finally, the dictator pushes that master branch to a blessed reference repository for all others to use.
